title: Path pullbacks recognize cartesian squares in the coherent nerve of Kan complexes
statement:
Use spaces, coherent squares, cones and weak homotopy equivalences of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and the subset-poset coherent nerve of [def-coef-coherent-nerve-infrastructure]. Let $\mathsf{Kan}$ be the simplicial category of small Kan complexes with function simplicial sets, and let $\mathcal S=N_{\mathrm{hc}}(\mathsf{Kan})$. For Kan complexes $A,B,C,D$ and a strictly commuting square with top $f:A\to B$, left $g:A\to C$, right $r:B\to D$, bottom $s:C\to D$, put
$$P=B\times_{D,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,D)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,D}C.$$
Let $q:A\to P$ have coordinates $f,g$ and the constant path at $rf=sg$. The strict square, regarded as a coherent square in $\mathcal S$, is cartesian in the limiting-cone sense if and only if $q$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. The assertion also holds for a specified homotopy-commuting square: a simplicial map $H:A\times\Delta^1\to D$ from $rf$ to $sg$ specifies $q$ by its path coordinate, and the coherent square must carry that commutation datum, including its triangle witnesses. Cartesian squares in $\mathcal S$ are invariant under equivalences of whole coherent square diagrams: an equivalence in $\operatorname{Fun}(N([1]\times[1]),\mathcal S)$ preserves and reflects cartesianness. In particular, for any objectwise weak-equivalence zigzag of strict Kan-complex square diagrams, or any equivalence between a coherent square and such a strict presentation, cartesianness is equivalent to the strict presentation being homotopy cartesian. The path model and the comparison use the given commutation data; equality only of their four vertices or edge homotopy classes is not sufficient.

source.place: Theorem 6.1.4 and its converse Theorem 6.2.7, printed pp.43–52, specialized to the cospan Λ²₂; path-pullback pseudo-weighted limit and equivalence invariance of limiting cones. proof.text: Work in a containing universe for the simplicial category of small Kan complexes. Its mapping simplicial sets are Kan, and $\mathcal S=N_{\mathrm{hc}}(\mathsf{Kan})$ is a quasicategory by [lem-coef-kan-coherent-nerve-quasicategory]. Apply [lem-coef-space-path-fibration-replacement] to $r:B\to D$: $E_r=B\times_{D,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,D)\to D$, evaluated at $1$, is a Kan fibration. Its pullback $P=E_r\times_D C$ is Kan: a horn lifting problem in $P\to C$ is a lifting problem for that fibration, and then a horn in $P$ is filled by first filling its image in the Kan complex $C$. The adjoint $\widehat H:A\to\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,D)$, together with $f,g$, defines $q$ because its two evaluations are $rf,sg$. Constant $H$ gives exactly the strict comparison in the statement.

source.place: Example 3.1.8.10 (0101), path fibration; the horn argument for its pullback is written here.

proof.text:
Fix a small Kan complex $X$ and abbreviate $T_Y=\operatorname{Fun}(X,Y)$. The internal-Hom definition gives a degreewise currying isomorphism
$$T_P\cong T_B\times_{T_D,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,T_D)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,T_D}T_C=:P_T.$$
Indeed, a map $X\times\Delta^n\to P$ is precisely two maps to $B,C$ and a map $X\times\Delta^n\times\Delta^1\to D$ with the prescribed endpoint restrictions; switching the last two factors gives the displayed formula. Restriction in $[n]$ commutes with this bijection, so it is simplicial. Under it, $T_q:T_A\to P_T$ sends $a$ to $(fa,ga,H\circ(a\times\mathrm{id}_{\Delta^1}))$. All $T_Y$ occurring here are Kan by [lem-cbc-kan-functor-space-kan], including $T_P$.

source.place: Finite cospan specialization of the enriched testing in Theorems 6.1.4 and 6.2.7; the currying calculation is agent-written.

proof.text:
Put $R_Y=\operatorname{Map}^R_{\mathcal S}(X,Y)$, with the right-pinched convention of the statement. These spaces are Kan by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. The comparison [lem-coef-point-family-q-counit-identification] supplies homotopy equivalences $\alpha_Y:T_Y\to R_Y$, given in degree $n$ by precomposition with $q^n:Q^n\to\Delta^n$. Postcomposition by either fixed map $r$ or $s$ commutes strictly with this formula. Apply [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance] to these three vertical weak equivalences, on $T_B\to T_D\leftarrow T_C$. It gives a weak equivalence
$$v_X:P_T\longrightarrow R_B\times^h_{R_D}R_C=:P_R.$$
The hypotheses are the strict postcomposition identities just checked and the Kan conditions on $T_B,T_C,T_D,R_B,R_C,R_D$.

source.place: Example 4.6.7.7 and Remark 4.6.7.6 (enriched mapping comparison); Proposition 3.4.0.9 (032B), invariance of path pullbacks.

proof.text:
Let $c_X:R_A\to P_R$ be the comparison of the specified coherent square. Use $U_Y=U_{\mathcal S}(X,Y)$ and $j_Y:R_Y\to U_Y$ from [lem-coef-infinity-pinch-comparison]. These are Kan spaces and homotopy equivalences. Fixed enriched postcomposition by $r,s$ commutes with $j$: in each simplex it changes the target row, whereas $j$ precomposes the domain by the pinch. Thus [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance] gives a weak equivalence $w_X:P_R\to P_U$, where $P_U=U_B\times^h_{U_D}U_C$. The parameterized composition clause of [lem-coef-point-family-q-counit-identification], applied to $\beta=j\alpha$, gives
$$w_Xc_X\alpha_A\simeq w_Xv_XT_q.$$
The projection coordinates are $\beta_B(fa),\beta_C(ga)$; the path coordinate is $\beta_D(H\circ(a\times\mathrm{id}))$, with its endpoint composition homotopies and the square's two triangle witnesses. Naturality in the additional simplex parameter of $a$ makes this a homotopy of entire maps into $P_U$, retaining the path coordinate. This asserts compatibility in the arrow model where the cited composition clause is stated, without assuming strict compatibility for $\alpha$ alone. Homotopic maps have the same weak-equivalence status: their cylinder projection contracts by interval minimum, hence is a weak equivalence by [lem-cbc-simplicial-homotopy-equivalence-weak]; its endpoint sections are weak equivalences by the model two-out-of-three property of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-model-right-proper-core]. Apply two-out-of-three to the homotopy. Since $w_X,\alpha_A,v_X$ are weak equivalences, $c_X$ is a weak equivalence exactly when $T_q$ is.

source.place: Example 4.6.7.7, Remark 4.6.7.6; parameterized composition normalization as stated in lem-coef-point-family-q-counit-identification. Agent specialization retaining H and the triangle witnesses.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-coef-infinity-terminal-pullback-criterion] in the quasicategory $\mathcal S$. It asserts that this specified coherent square is limiting exactly when $c_X$ is a weak equivalence for every object $X$. Every object of $\mathcal S$ is a small Kan complex. Steps 2--4 therefore turn its criterion into
$$\text{the square is cartesian}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{Fun}(X,q)\text{ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every small Kan }X.$$
No assumption of connectedness or nonemptiness has entered this reduction.

source.place: Theorem 6.6.9 and Remark 6.6.11, specialized through the existing mapping-space criterion; compare Riehl--Verity Theorem 6.2.7, proof on printed p.52.

proof.text: Suppose $q$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Both $A$ and $P$ are Kan by hypothesis and step 1, so [lem-cbc-kan-whitehead-inverse] supplies $u:P\to A$ and simplicial homotopies $uq\simeq\mathrm{id}_A$, $qu\simeq\mathrm{id}_P$. Postcomposition gives an inverse $\operatorname{Fun}(X,u)$ for $\operatorname{Fun}(X,q)$ up to simplicial homotopy: a homotopy $J:Y\times\Delta^1\to Y$ induces $(a,t)\mapsto J(a(-),t)$ on $\operatorname{Fun}(X,Y)\times\Delta^1$. By [lem-cbc-simplicial-homotopy-equivalence-weak] each $\operatorname{Fun}(X,q)$ is a weak equivalence. Step 5 proves cartesianness. Conversely, if the square is cartesian, step 5 applies at $X=\Delta^0$. Evaluation gives simplicial isomorphisms $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^0,A)=A$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^0,P)=P$, and under these the tested map is exactly $q$. Hence $q$ is a weak equivalence. This proves both directions for the strict and the specified-homotopy cases.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.7.13 (00UB), both directions; exponentiation of the actual inverse homotopies is written here.

proof.text: An equivalence of whole coherent square diagrams restricts to an equivalence of their lower cospans and has an equivalence as its apex component; the compatibility of these restrictions is the map of cones supplied by the original coherent transformation. The invariance and naturality clauses of [lem-coef-infinity-terminal-pullback-criterion] therefore preserve and reflect its mapping-space test. It follows that cartesianness is invariant under an equivalence in $\operatorname{Fun}(N([1]\times[1]),\mathcal S)$. Applying the same argument to its inverse gives reflection, not just preservation. This argument applies also to coherent squares not presented by strict simplicial maps.

source.place: Theorem 6.6.9, cone criterion and its naturality, applied to an equivalence of coherent cones; agent spelling out of the invariance clause of the cited node.

proof.text: For a weak homotopy equivalence $e:U\to V$ of Kan complexes, [lem-cbc-kan-whitehead-inverse] provides $d$ and homotopies $de\simeq\mathrm{id}_U$, $ed\simeq\mathrm{id}_V$. Each is an edge in the appropriate function complex. By the subset-poset definition of the coherent nerve, a $2$-simplex is three edges together with a path from the diagonal edge to their composite. Thus these homotopies, oriented from the identity to the composite if necessary by filling a Kan $2$-horn with the original edge and a degenerate edge, give the two inverse triangles for $e$ in $\mathcal S$. Hence $e$ is an equivalence edge. A strict natural transformation of strict square diagrams gives a coherent transformation after applying the ordinary-to-coherent nerve map (all strict commutation witnesses are constant). If it is objectwise a weak equivalence, its components are equivalences as just proved, so [lem-coef-infinity-pointwise-equivalences] makes the entire transformation an equivalence. Apply step 7 along the zigzag and steps 5--6 to each strict presentation. This gives precisely the claimed strict homotopy-cartesian test, also when an arbitrary coherent square is equivalent to the strict presentation.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.7.13; Theorem 4.4.4.4 (01DK); the inverse triangles are read directly from the subset-poset coherent nerve.

proof.text: Throughout the construction the map into the path factor is the adjoint of the prescribed $H$; in the strict case it is the constant path at $rf=sg$. Step 4 uses the specified triangle witnesses when comparing this map with the coherent cone test. Step 7 transports the entire coherent square. Replacing these data by their vertex list or by the homotopy classes of the four boundary edges would discard exactly the path coordinate used in steps 2 and 4, so none of those replacements is made.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.7 proof, comparison induced by the actual cone; reminder of the fixed commutation data in the present specialization.
